title: 301 vs 302 Redirects: Which to Use and How to Fix Chains
excerpt: Learn the real difference between 301 and 302 redirects, when 307 and 308 fit, and how to clean up redirect chains, loops and meta refresh after a migration.
meta_title: 301 vs 302 Redirect: When to Use Each for SEO
meta_description: 301 vs 302 redirect explained: what each tells Google, when to use 307 or 308, and how to find and fix redirect chains, loops and meta refresh redirects.
key_takeaways: Google treats 301 and 308 redirects as permanent and uses them as a signal that the target URL should be canonical.
A 302 or 307 tells Google the move is temporary, so the original URL tends to stay in search results.
Some server rules and code default to 302, so always check the actual status code of a permanent move.
Redirect chains and loops waste requests and slow visitors down, so point every redirect straight at the final URL.
After a migration, map old URLs one to one, update internal links and sitemaps, and keep redirects live for at least a year.
content_html:
You changed a URL, added a redirect, and moved on. Months later the old address still turns up in search results, or a crawl shows that half your internal links pass through two or three hops before they reach a real page. Nothing is technically broken, but nothing is clean either.

Most of these problems trace back to one decision made in a hurry: the 301 vs 302 redirect choice. A 301 says "this page has moved for good." A 302 says "this page is somewhere else for now." Google treats those two messages differently, so the code you pick changes which URL ends up in search results.

In this guide you will learn what each redirect code tells Google, when 307 and 308 make more sense, how redirect chains and loops form, why meta refresh is a fallback rather than a plan, and how to clean everything up after a site migration. If you are working through a full technical SEO audit checklist, this is the redirects step in detail.

What a redirect actually tells Google

A redirect is an HTTP response that says "the thing you asked for lives at another URL." The browser or crawler then requests the new address. Visitors rarely notice which type of redirect you used. Google does.

According to Google's documentation on redirects, a permanent redirect is a signal that the target URL should become canonical, while a temporary redirect is not. In plain terms, a permanent redirect tends to put the new URL in search results, and a temporary one tends to keep the old URL there.

Say you rename /services/web-design to /services/website-design. With a 301, Google is told the new URL is the one to keep, so over time it swaps the address shown in results. With a 302, Google is told the move is temporary, which gives it a reason to keep showing the old address.

What to do:

  • Decide whether the move is permanent before you choose a code.
  • If you will never switch back, use a permanent redirect.
  • If the original URL will return, use a temporary one.

301 vs 302 redirect: the comparison table

There are four redirect codes worth knowing. Two are permanent, two are temporary, and within each pair the difference is about how the browser treats the request method.

CodeTypeHow Google treats itRequest methodTypical use
301 Moved PermanentlyPermanentTarget is a strong canonical candidateGET stays GET, other methods may switch to GETChanged slugs, HTTPS moves, domain changes, merged pages
308 Permanent RedirectPermanentSame as 301Method and body preservedPermanent moves where forms or APIs send POST requests
302 FoundTemporaryNot used as a canonical signalGET stays GET, other methods may switch to GETShort-term detours, maintenance notices
307 Temporary RedirectTemporarySame as 302Method and body preservedTemporary moves where non-GET requests must survive

The method column comes from the HTTP specification and is summarized clearly in MDN's guide to HTTP redirections. On an ordinary content site, where browsers and crawlers mostly send GET requests, 301 and 308 behave the same for SEO, and so do 302 and 307. Google groups 301 and 308 as permanent, and 302, 303 and 307 as temporary.

For most site owners the rule is simple: use a 301 for permanent moves and a 302 for genuinely temporary ones. Reach for 308 or 307 when a developer needs the request method preserved, such as a form endpoint that moved.

When to use a 301 (or 308)

Use a permanent redirect whenever the old URL is not coming back. Common cases:

  • You changed a page's slug or folder structure.
  • You moved from HTTP to HTTPS, or picked www over non-www.
  • You merged two thin pages into one stronger page.
  • You retired a product and have a direct replacement.
  • You moved the whole site to a new domain.

Say you run a bakery site with 40 pages, and you merge "Wedding Cakes" and "Custom Wedding Cakes" into one page. The URL that disappears gets a 301 to the one that stays, so anyone following an old link or bookmark lands on the merged page.

One caution: redirect to the closest equivalent page, not to your home page. Sending every retired URL to the home page confuses visitors who expected something specific. If a page is gone with no replacement, a 404 or 410 is the honest answer. If you are unsure which applies, here is how to decide between restoring, redirecting, or letting a page 404.

When to use a 302 (or 307)

A temporary redirect is right when you want visitors sent elsewhere for a while, but you want the original URL to keep its place in search. Google's own example is a service that is temporarily unavailable: you redirect to a page explaining the situation without giving up the original URL in results.

Other fair uses include a booking page sent to a "back soon" notice during a system upgrade, or a product page sent to a holding page while stock is replaced. In each case the original URL will serve real content again.

The far more common mistake runs the other way: a permanent move that was set up as a 302 by accident. Some tools default to temporary. Apache's Redirect directive returns a 302 unless you specify otherwise, and so does PHP's header('Location: ...') on its own. Many CMS redirect plugins let you pick the type, and it is easy to leave the wrong option selected.

Check the actual status code rather than trusting the settings screen. From a terminal:

curl -I https://example.com/old-page

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://example.com/new-page

If you see 302 Found on a move you meant to be permanent, change the rule to a 301 and recheck.

Redirect chains and loops

A redirect chain is when one redirect leads to another before reaching a page that returns 200. Chains usually build up over years, one sensible change at a time. Here is a typical one:

  1. http://example.com/blog/post redirects to the HTTPS version.
  2. https://example.com/blog/post redirects to the www version.
  3. https://www.example.com/blog/post redirects to the version with a trailing slash.
  4. https://www.example.com/blog/post/ finally returns the page.

Each hop is another round trip for the visitor's browser and another request for a crawler. Google's site move guidelines say Googlebot can follow up to 10 hops, but advise redirecting straight to the final destination and, if a chain is unavoidable, keeping it to no more than 3 hops and fewer than 5. They also note that chains add latency and that not every browser handles long chains.

A redirect loop is worse: A redirects to B, and B redirects back to A. The page never loads for anyone. Loops often appear when two rules disagree, for example a server rule that adds a trailing slash and a CMS setting that removes it. Search Console reports both long chains and loops as a "Redirect error" in the Page indexing report.

How to fix them:

  • List every redirect source and its final destination.
  • Rewrite each rule so the source points directly at the final 200 URL.
  • Order your rules so protocol and host fixes happen in a single hop, not three.
  • Test a sample of old URLs and confirm one 301 followed by a 200.

Internal links that point at redirects

Even a single, correct 301 is a detour when it sits behind your own internal links. If your navigation links to /services/web-design and that URL redirects, every visit and every crawl takes an extra step to reach a page you control.

Your own links should point at the final URL, not at a redirect. Redirects are there to catch old bookmarks and links from other sites, not to patch your own navigation.

Say your footer, three blog posts and a services menu all link to an old URL. Update all five links to the new address and the redirect becomes a safety net that your own site never needs. Apply the same rule to your sitemap: list only final URLs, never redirecting ones, and keep your XML sitemap clean after any URL change.

Finding these by hand is slow on anything bigger than a handful of pages. A free desktop crawler like Scary Spider SEO flags internal redirects, long redirect chains and meta refresh redirects in one crawl, so you can export the list and fix the links at the source.

Meta refresh and JavaScript redirects

Sometimes you cannot touch server settings, for example on a locked-down hosting plan. Two fallbacks exist, and both are second best.

A meta refresh is an HTML tag in the page head, such as <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=https://example.com/new">. Google interprets an instant meta refresh (0 seconds) as a permanent redirect and a delayed one as a temporary redirect. MDN also recommends keeping the delay at 0 for accessibility, because a page that jumps after a few seconds can disorient visitors.

A JavaScript redirect sets window.location in a script. Google says to use it only if server-side and meta refresh redirects are not possible, because Google only sees it after rendering the page, and rendering can fail.

Use a server-side 301 whenever you can, and treat meta refresh and JavaScript as fallbacks. If a crawl shows meta refresh redirects you did not create on purpose, they often come from old landing page builders or a theme setting, and are worth replacing.

A redirect cleanup process after a site migration

Migrations are where redirects go wrong at scale: a new CMS, a new URL structure, or a new domain. Work through these steps in order.

  1. Capture every old URL before you switch. Combine a full crawl, your current sitemap, and the top landing pages from Search Console and your analytics.
  2. Map each old URL to its closest new equivalent. One to one wherever possible. Keep the map in a spreadsheet with columns for old URL, new URL and status.
  3. Implement the map as server-side 301s. Avoid sending large groups of unrelated URLs to the home page.
  4. Test the old URL list after launch. Every row should return a single 301 to a page that returns 200. Fix chains, loops and 404s now.
  5. Update everything you control. Internal links, canonical tags, your sitemap, and hreflang tags if you use them should all reference the new URLs directly.
  6. Leave the redirects in place. Google's site move guidance says to keep them for as long as possible, generally at least one year, so signals and external links can be reassigned to the new URLs.
  7. Monitor Search Console. "Page with redirect" for old URLs is expected. "Redirect error" and a rising count of 404s are not, and need attention.

Say a 60-page site moves from /index.php?page=about style URLs to clean paths like /about. The map has 60 rows, the test takes minutes with a crawler in list mode or a short script, and the payoff is that every old link, bookmark and search result still lands somewhere useful.

The bottom line

The 301 vs 302 redirect decision comes down to one question: is the old URL ever coming back? If not, use a 301 (or 308) so Google moves its attention to the new page. If it is, use a 302 (or 307) and keep the original URL in place.

After that, keep it tidy. One hop from old to new, internal links and sitemaps pointing at final URLs, no accidental meta refresh, and redirects that stay live for at least a year after a migration.

Your next step: run curl -I on five URLs you have changed in the past year, confirm each returns a single 301 to a live page, and fix any that return a 302 or pass through more than one hop.

faqs.question: Do 301 redirects pass link equity?
faqs.answer: Google uses a permanent redirect as a strong signal that the target URL should be canonical, and signals for duplicate URLs are consolidated onto the canonical. In practice a clean, one-hop 301 to a closely matching page is the standard way to move a page without starting over. Chains and redirects to unrelated pages are where problems start.

faqs.question: How long should I keep a 301 redirect in place?
faqs.answer: Google's site move guidance says to keep redirects for as long as possible, and generally at least one year. If old URLs still receive links or visits after that, there is little reason to remove them.

faqs.question: Will a 302 redirect hurt my rankings?
faqs.answer: A 302 is not a penalty. The risk is that a permanent move set up as a 302 tells Google the old URL should stay in results, which can leave the wrong address showing. If the move is permanent, switch it to a 301.

faqs.question: Is a 308 redirect better than a 301 for SEO?
faqs.answer: Google treats 301 and 308 the same way, as permanent redirects. The difference is technical: a 308 guarantees the browser keeps the original request method, which matters for forms and APIs. For normal page moves either works.

faqs.question: How can I tell which type of redirect a page uses?
faqs.answer: Run curl -I on the old URL in a terminal and read the status line, or open your browser's developer tools and check the Network tab. A site crawler will also report the status code and final destination for every redirecting URL it finds.
